5:The question. Climb batch 7C rewrote the traits chapter to the type group's 2012 reading of a `comprises` clause: the clause says to which types a trait's values belong, and a trait with static parameters may stand unlisted between a closed trait and its listed types when every trait or object extending it is below a listed type (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:235-252`). Four passages elsewhere still argue from a clause at the level of types: the intersection example (P1, `basic/types-vals-vars.tex:583-604`), the Meet Rule's example (P2, `advanced/overloading.tex:275-307`), the rule on abstract function declarations (P3, `basic/functions.tex:370-415`) and a team draft note (P4, `basic/components/source-code.tex:428-434`). Row 491 asks whether they still hold and what the specification and the two implementations should do. The clean worker's note (`reviews/comprises-type-level-ways.md`, "the ways note" below) lists six ways and marks its own reading. This note checks the deciding claims at their sources, adds one measurement, weighs the ways and recommends one.
11:- `trait S comprises { U, V }` closes `S`. The type reading: every type under `S` is under `U` or `V`. This was the Working Draft's note and it is Java's `sealed`. The value reading, "coverage": every value of `S` is a value of `U` or `V`. This is the 2012 Types chapter and Welterweight, and batch 7C's text. A trait has no values of its own; only objects make values. So under the value reading a trait may sit between `S` and its listed types, and it is a type below `S` and below no listed type.
12:- P1 and P2 conclude "any subtype of both S and T must be a subtype of V. Thus, V = S ∩ T" from the clauses of `S` and `T` and `U excludes W`. That first step needs the type reading. Under the value reading the same steps show that every value of both `S` and `T` is a value of `V`: `V` covers `S ∩ T`.

59fdeff62 2012-06-06 Guy Steele
Fixed TypeAnalyzer (pSubInner) so that when asking the question A <: B union C where A has a comprises clause { D, E }, one of the questions it asks is whether D union E <: B union C.  This should improve the behavior of 'covers' checks in AbstractMethodChecker

===== Welterweight

The rule \rncite{T-Program} verifies that no two declarations are identical, that declared traits and objects all have distinct names,
and that the declaratins and the expression are well-formed.  It also verifies that any abstract function declarations are ````covered''
by concrete implementations.  The notion of ````covering'' is a generalization of the notion of ````overriding,'' because an abstract function
with an argument that is a trait type with a comprises clause
is considered to be covered if it is implemented for all the types comprised.
For example:
\[
\begin{array}{@{}l@{}}
\kwd{trait}\;\mathrm{Color}\ob{} \extends \set{\,} \comprises \set{\mathrm{Red}\ob{}, \mathrm{Green}\ob{}} \exc \set{\,} \; \kwd{end} \\[1pt]
\kwd{trait}\;\mathrm{Green}\ob{}() \extends \set{\mathrm{Color}\ob{}} \kwd{end} \\[1pt]
\kwd{trait}\;\mathrm{Red}\ob{}() \extends \set{\mathrm{Color}\ob{}} \kwd{end} \\[1pt]
\mathrm{toggle}\ob{}\bigtuple{x: \mathrm{Color}\ob{}}: \mathrm{Color}\ob{} \\[1pt]
\mathrm{toggle}\ob{}\bigtuple{y: \mathrm{Green}\ob{}}: \mathrm{Color}\ob{} = \mathrm{Red}\ob{}() \\[1pt]
\mathrm{toggle}\ob{}\bigtuple{y: \mathrm{Red}\ob{}}: \mathrm{Color}\ob{} = \mathrm{Green}\ob{}()
\end{array}
\]
The abstract function $\mathrm{toggle}$ that takes an argument of type $\mathrm{Color}\ob{}$ is considered to be implemented
by the two concrete definitions of $\mathrm{toggle}$ because they collectively accept all the types comprised by $\mathrm{Color}\ob{}$.
The rules for checking such covering are actually more general than that, and appear in Figure~\ref{fig:covered}.
The basic idea is that the domain type of an abstract function (the tuple of argument types, with any type parameters of the function existentially quantified~\cite{oopsla-2011-type-checking})
must be a subtype of the union of the domains of the concrete definitions.  The function $\noselfdom$ is used to compute these domain types;
the wrinkle is that the same rules are used to check methods as well as functions, and for methods, the type of the trait of object within which
the method is declared is \emph{not} considered for the purposes of this particular test.

The rule \rncite{T-Program} furthermore ensure that the function declarations obey the No Duplicates Rule, the Meet Rule,

# Walk's two load readings, checked against the specification and the team's library

## 1. What was checked, and against what

Climb batch 12's rung W made walk refuse at load an object that inherits an abstract method and gives it no body (row 649), and an `override` that overrides nothing (row 653's walk half). Two readings landed with it, each below the traits chapter's letter, each listed for the curator (`explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md:656-657`, `:670`; `explorations/reviews/batch-12-review.md:173-174`, `:325-327`):

- **Q1.** A declaration with a body whose parameter types are each at or below the abstract method's counts as defining it (the worker's decision 2, `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-walk-load-checks/REPORT.md:195-199`; row 666).
- **Q2.** "Overrides" includes an inherited declaration with equal parameter types (decision 4, `REPORT.md:205`), against the chapter's "strict subtype".

The standards, in the record's order: the specification, with the Types chapter beside it where it speaks (POSITIONS, "The specification stays the standard, the Types chapter beside it."); the type group's late positions, which outweigh earlier text where they differ (`.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/specification.md`, "Weighing the sources"); and the library's own practice (POSITIONS, "The library's own practice is the standard."). For each reading: what landed, exactly; what each source says; the verdict; what a replacement would change in the library, the tests and the demos; and the default.

## 2. Q1: a body at narrower parameter types defines an inherited abstract method

### 2.1 What landed

`Constructor.checkForDef` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/Constructor.java:423-453`) refuses an object, or an object expression, without static parameters that inherits a declaration without a body, unless `definedBelow` (`:466-484`) finds, among what the object's traits provide, one declaration with a body of the same name and self position whose parameter types are each a subtype, equality included, of the abstract declaration's. One such body is enough: nothing asks that the bodies together cover the abstract declaration's parameter types. A body whose parameter types walk cannot read counts too (`:480-482`). The residue is gated by `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXAbstractMethodPartlyDefinedWalk.fss` (row 666: `tag(self, x: ZZ32) = 1` under the abstract `tag(self, x: Number)` loads). The record states it so (FACTS, "Walk refuses at load an object that leaves an inherited abstract method without a body, ..."; PLAN, "Pavol's answers", item 51, and `PLAN.md:116`).

### 2.2 The chapter's letter

- A trait inherits the method declarations its immediate supertraits provide, "except those method declarations that are overridden ... or whose parameter type (not including the type of the self parameter) is equal to the parameter type of a method declaration that occurs in the trait declaration" (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:519-526`).
- "An abstract method declaration declares an abstract method; any object inheriting an abstract method must define a body expression for the method" (`:570-572`; the Working Draft of February 2011 has the same words, `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/traits.tex:511`, and so does the 1.0 release).

Read literally, as the worker read it (`REPORT.md:121-128`, section 5): an object whose own declarations are at narrower types has none with the abstract declaration's parameter type, so it inherits the abstract declaration and must define it; a narrower body, alone or with others, does not. That refuses the landed allowance and the coverage shape alike.

The chapter is not of one mind, though. Its own sentence on functional methods says "An abstract function declaration ... can be provided also for overloaded functional method declarations" (`:558-560`), and the rule for abstract function declarations, as the revival revised it under the type group's reading of a `comprises` clause, asks for coverage: "the argument types of the concrete declarations for f must together cover T", "a definition for every type listed in the comprises clause of Molecule, or definitions that together cover those types, or it is a static error" (`Specification/basic/functions.tex:386-395`, `:431-434`, the callouts `revival-covering` at `:396-400` and `:435-444`). The Meet Rule has its covering case in the same words (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:312-336`). Only the sentence at `traits.tex:570-572` is older than that reading.

### 2.3 The team's later word

- **The compiled checker, Guy Steele, May 2012.** `AbstractMethodChecker.checkObjectDeclaration` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/AbstractMethodChecker.scala:88-118`, the comment "GLS 5/30/12" inside it): "For each abstract method, check to see whether it is covered by one or more concrete definitions." It takes the concrete declarations of the name and self position whose domains are below the abstract one's, joins their domains into a union, and refuses the object unless the abstract domain is a subtype of that union. A lone narrower body fails it; narrower bodies that together cover pass it.
- **His next commit, 59fdeff62, 2012-06-06**: `TypeAnalyzer` reads a `comprises` clause when it asks whether a closed trait is below a union, "This should improve the behavior of 'covers' checks in AbstractMethodChecker" (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:152-157`). So the checker's coverage reads `comprises` clauses, on purpose, since June 2012. The worker measured it: `CoverAbstractProbe`, the shape of `trait D comprises { P, Q }` with abstract `f(self, other: D)` and `P` declaring `f` over `P` and over `Q`, type checks (exit 0), and `PartAbstractProbe`, row 666's program, is refused, "Domain Number is not a subtype of ZZ32" (`REPORT.md:147-148`).
- **Welterweight Fortress, 2012.** The Covered judgement: "The notion of 'covering' is a generalization of the notion of 'overriding,' because an abstract function with an argument that is a trait type with a comprises clause is considered to be covered if it is implemented for all the types comprised"; "the domain type of an abstract function ... must be a subtype of the union of the domains of the concrete definitions"; and "the same rules are used to check methods as well as functions, and for methods, the type of the trait or object within which the method is declared is not considered" (`Papers/Welterweight/static.tick:27-47`; the rule, `Papers/Welterweight/fig-covered.tick:9-13`).
- **The internal FAQ**: "An abstract method can be implemented by concrete methods whose return types are subtypes of the abstract method" (`Specification/appendices/FAQ.tex:159-162`), several concrete methods for one abstract one.
- **The later restart** says nothing: its Types, traits, declarations, objects and overloading chapters hold neither "abstract" nor "override" (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/*.tick`).
- **The team's walk** never made the check: its `checkForDef` returned for every `FnDecl`, body or not (`Constructor.java:398-403` at `a874948ac`), which is row 649.

By the record's weighing, the checker's rule and Welterweight's are the type group's late position, written by the team member who wrote the chapter; they outweigh the sentence at `traits.tex:570-572`.

### 2.4 The team's library and tests

- `Library/Pairs.fss:77-87`: `trait RunRanges comprises { SingleRange, RangeSet }` with abstract `opr BOXPLUS(self, x: RunRanges)`; `SingleRange` defines `BOXPLUS` over `SingleRange` and over `RangeSet`, and `RangeSet` likewise. On the batch's merged tree the one library loads without the allowance only until `Pairs` is imported (the gather's gather.1, `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-12/RECORD.md:222`).
- `ProjectFortress/tests/FileConversion.fss:66-82`, the team's test, in the suite: `trait dna comprises { dnaSequence, EmptySequence }` with abstract `opr OPLUS(self, other: dna)`, `dnaSequence` defining it over `dnaSequence` and over `EmptySequence`. The same shape.

### 2.5 Verdict

The landed reading is a stopgap, not a reading of any team source. It is wider than the checker's rule, since a lone narrower body satisfies it, and outside the chapter's letter, which admits no narrower body. The rule that should hold is the one the team wrote last, the Covered rule: an object defines an inherited abstract method when its declarations with bodies of that name and self position, at parameter types below the abstract one's, together cover the abstract one's parameter types, `comprises` clauses read as the checker reads them since 59fdeff62. A lone body at the abstract declaration's own parameter types is the trivial cover, so the chapter's plain case is inside it. That is way (a) of Q1's entry, sharpened: the test is coverage, whether or not a `comprises` clause supplies it. It is the type group's word of 2012, it is what the chapter already says of abstract functions and of overloaded functional methods, and it is what the team's library (`Pairs`) and the team's test (`FileConversion`) do. Way (b), the letter, is ruled out: it refuses both, and the checker.

Building it: in walk, `definedBelow` gathers every body below the abstract declaration and tests coverage with `OverloadedFunction.overlapPieces` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:1023`), walk's reader of `comprises` clauses for the Meet Rule, rather than returning at the first body; in the specification, `traits.tex:570-572` through the revision form, in the words `functions.tex:431-434` already uses. The same entry should correct a sentence the revival wrote that this check shows false: "The compiled type checker checks, at each object declaration, that the object's concrete methods cover the abstract methods it inherits, reading no comprises clause" (`functions.tex:441-443`; `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:2604-2606`). It reads one, by 59fdeff62 and by the worker's `CoverAbstractProbe`; the comprises judgement had already noted Steele's rule (`explorations/reviews/comprises-type-level-judgement.md:21`).

### 2.6 What replacing it would change

With the Covered rule in place of the allowance, on the merged tree:

- Accepted as today: `Pairs` (`RunRanges` is covered by `SingleRange` and `RangeSet` through its clause), `FileConversion.fss`, and the 20 demos that import `Pairs` (`BirdCount1q` to `BirdCount2d`).

So the coverage rule can land only after rows 668 and 669 are repaired in the library, the order PLAN gives ("before row 666 is tightened"); by reading, 669's repair is of rung G's kind for row 628, the `Any` device replaced by the implementer's shape, and 668's is a body at `Generator[\ZZ32\]`. Both are a library rung's to design from the library's own way.

### 2.7 Default

As landed: walk's allowance, row 666 open, until rows 668 and 669 are repaired; then the Covered rule, with the chapter's sentence revised. Q1's entry says so already. It stands, and the answer to its question is (a) in the form above.

## 3. Q2: an `override` with equal parameter types overrides

### 3.1 What landed

`Constructor.checkOverrides` (`Constructor.java:555-576`) refuses an own declaration with the modifier `override` of an object, or of a trait without static parameters, that `overriddenBy` (`:615-634`) relates to none of the declarations its immediate supertraits provide; a generic or unreadable inherited declaration of the name counts as overridden. `overriddenBy` asks that each parameter type of the inherited declaration be a subtype of the override's, equality included. So `object B extends A` with `override f(x: ZZ32)` over `A`'s `f(x: ZZ32)` loads. The same non-strict relation drops inherited declarations in `providedByTrait` (`:528-530`), and `FunctionalMethodMeets.inherited` folds the equal clause and the override clause into one test (`OverloadedFunction.java:1211-1233`). No ledger row gates the equal-typed case (no row's text holds it), and no test writes it; PLAN's Q2 entry is its only record.

### 3.2 The chapter's letter

"A method declaration may have the modifier override. Such a declaration overrides any inherited declaration with the same name and the self parameter (if any) at the same position, whose parameter type, not counting the type of the self parameter, is a strict subtype of the overriding declaration's parameter type. ... A declaration with the modifier override must override some inherited declaration. It is a static error if a declaration with the modifier override does not override any inherited declaration" (`traits.tex:585-595`; the frozen copy, `:529`, `:535`, the same). The inheritance rule's second clause (`:523-526`) is the complement: a declaration with equal parameter types hides the inherited one without overriding it. So an equal-typed `override` hides by `:523-526`, overrides nothing by `:589`, and is a static error by `:594-595`. The letter is unambiguous.

Its history makes it deliberate. The 1.0 release of March 2008 (`Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf`, its text extracted) holds `override` only in the grammar and in the calculus's judgement on method overriding, which is redefinition at equal types with no modifier; it has no paragraph on the modifier. The team's internal list asks, under "overriding (03/10/08)", after an example in which `B`'s `override m(x: Object)` widens `A`'s `m(x: ZZ)`: "Do we want to allow to have override when the parameter types of the two declarations are the same?" (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:160-184`). The paragraph was written after that question, with "strict", and the question was never marked answered. The chapter's note says the modifier itself was "not yet supported" (`traits.tex:15-16`).

### 3.3 The team's later word

None. The later restart holds no text on the modifier (the keyword list and the BNF only). Welterweight has no modifier and calls covering "a generalization of the notion of 'overriding'" (`Papers/Welterweight/static.tick:28`). The Dispatch paper: "in Fortress overriding is merely a special case of overloading because the type of the receiver object is taken into account" (`Papers/Dispatch/body.tex:789-792`). Nothing outweighs the chapter here.

### 3.4 The implementations

- The team's checker never read the modifier (no `isOverride` in `scala_src` at `a874948ac`); the team's walk read it by name, dropping an object's inherited declarations of that name (`Constructor.java:442-474` at `a874948ac`, `newOverrides`).
- The revival's checker reads inheritance by the chapter: `providedAndOverridden` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:1651-1700`) tests equality first, `equivalentED`, and marks the pair `equal` without consulting the modifier; only then, `isOverride && subtypeED`, an override (`excludes`, `:1662-1671`). Its return-type check treats an `equal` pair as an overloaded pair, both ways (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/OverloadingChecker.scala:656-677`). So the checker does not read an equal-typed `override` as overriding; it reads it as the equal clause. It has no check of the modifier at all, which is row 653's checker half, waiting on row 650. PLAN's Q2 entry, "Both paths read it as overriding", is exact for walk and not for the checker.
- Walk: as landed, non-strict in both the drop and the check.

### 3.5 The library and the tests

The library writes no `override`: none in `Library/*.fss`, `Library/*.fsi`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/` or `ProjectFortress/CompilerLibrary/` (the word occurs only in prose comments, `Library/Random.fss:22`, `:43`, `Library/ReflectiveQuickCheck.fss:107`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4164`).
